## claude.ai Linear
When passing string values to tools, send the content directly without escape sequences. For example, use real newlines in markdown content rather than literal backslash-n (\n) characters.

## plugin:datadog:mcp
This is an MCP server for Datadog (a software observability platform). Consult Datadog docs if you're unsure about how something works in the platform. Docs for this MCP server can be found at https://docs.datadoghq.com/bits_ai/mcp_server/setup/ This server ships skill guides containing domain-specific guidance, workflows, and best practices that are not visible in tool names or schemas. Before invoking other tools, always perform skill discovery by running both paths in parallel: a direct load with `load_datadog_skill` using a general domain name (e.g. skill_name='datadog/traces'), and a call to `list_datadog_skills` with a fuzzy `query` based on topic keywords — load any clearly matching result from the listing along with the related skills it points to. The exception is a follow-up call in a domain whose skill you have already loaded or confirmed absent this session. If nothing clearly fits, do not load a skill — proceed with the tool descriptions. When the user asks to visualize, chart, or graph data — or when loading a data domain skill (e.g. datadog/traces, datadog/logs, datadog/metrics) — also load datadog/visualizations. Investigation results often benefit from charts.

159	func contextReauthError(c *contexts.Context, err error) error {

186		mgr, err := newContextTokenManager(c, transport, allowInsecureHTTP)

188			return nil, err

190		return &RefreshingLoginCredential{context: c, manager: mgr}, nil
191	}

193	// Token returns a locally fresh login JWT, refreshing it when needed.
194	func (c *RefreshingLoginCredential) Token(ctx context.Context) (string, error) {
195		tok, err := c.manager.Refresh(ctx)
196		return c.result(tok, err)

200	// server despite still appearing locally valid.

207		if mapped := contextReauthError(c.context, err); mapped != nil {

217	// repocreds wants) for context c that transparently re-mints an expired login
218	// JWT from the stored refresh token. Call NewRefreshingLoginCredential when a
219	// reactive 401 path also needs to force-refresh a rejected token.

222	// against the server's single-use refresh-token rotation: refreshes are
223	// serialised across processes (an advisory file lock) and goroutines, the
224	// store is re-read after locking so a late waiter reuses a peer's freshly

20	// token carries no usable ExpiresAt. The server is the real authority; this
21	// only governs when local readers consider the cached token stale.
22	const defaultSavedTokenTTL = time.Hour

24	// contextTokenStore adapts one login context's keyring slots to auth-go's
25	// tokenstore.Store, so tokenmanager can load, refresh, and persist that
26	// context's credentials. It is bound to a specific (service, handle) at
27	// construction and ignores the profile argument: the cluster resolver has
28	// already chosen exactly one context, so there is no per-issuer account
29	// ambiguity to resolve here.
30	//
31	// Access token lives at `service`/`handle` (with the "|<expiry>" encoding
32	// the rest of the CLI reads); the refresh token lives raw at
33	// `service:refresh`/`handle`.
34	type contextTokenStore struct {
35		service string
36		handle  string
37	}

39	func (s contextTokenStore) LoadTokens(string) (tokens.TokenSet, error) {
40		enc, err := tokenstore.Get(s.service, s.handle)
41		// Map "no credential stored" to auth-go's sentinel so tokenmanager
42		// reports "not logged in" rather than a hard store failure.
43		if errors.Is(err, tokenstore.ErrNotFound) || (err == nil && enc == "") {
44			return tokens.TokenSet{}, authtokenstore.ErrNotFound
45		}
46		if err != nil {
47			return tokens.TokenSet{}, fmt.Errorf("read access token: %w", err)
48		}
49		access, expiresAt := tokenstore.DecodeTokenWithExpiration(enc)
50		// A missing refresh slot is fine (login predating offline_access) — treat
51		// it as no-refresh. Any other store error must surface, not be swallowed:
52		// dropping it would silently discard a valid refresh token and force a
53		// re-login on what was really a transient keyring/file-store failure.
54		refresh, err := tokenstore.Get(tokenstore.RefreshService(s.service), s.handle)
55		if err != nil && !errors.Is(err, tokenstore.ErrNotFound) {
56			return tokens.TokenSet{}, fmt.Errorf("read refresh token: %w", err)
57		}
58		return tokens.TokenSet{
59			AccessToken:  access,
60			RefreshToken: refresh,
61			ExpiresAt:    expiresAt,
62		}, nil
63	}
64	
65	func (s contextTokenStore) SaveTokens(_ string, t tokens.TokenSet) error {
66		if t.AccessToken == "" {
67			return errors.New("save tokens: empty access token")
68		}
69		expiresIn := int64(defaultSavedTokenTTL.Seconds())
70		if !t.ExpiresAt.IsZero() {
71			if secs := int64(time.Until(t.ExpiresAt).Seconds()); secs > 0 {
72				expiresIn = secs
73			}
74		}
75		// Persist the rotated refresh token BEFORE the access token. The server
76		// single-use-rotates refresh tokens, so a partial write must never leave
77		// a fresh access token paired with a stale refresh token: that pairing
78		// looks healthy until the access token expires, then the dead refresh
79		// token trips invalid_grant/family revocation and forces a re-login.
80		// Refresh-first inverts the failure modes: a failed refresh write aborts
81		// before touching the access slot (old pair preserved), and a failed
82		// access write after a good refresh write self-heals on the next load
83		// (the new refresh token re-mints an access token).
84		//
85		// persistRefreshed carries a still-valid refresh token forward when the
86		// server doesn't rotate, so an empty value here means "leave as-is",
87		// never "clear".
88		if t.RefreshToken != "" {
89			if err := tokenstore.Set(tokenstore.RefreshService(s.service), s.handle, t.RefreshToken); err != nil {
90				return fmt.Errorf("store refresh token: %w", err)
91			}
92		}
93		if err := tokenstore.Set(s.service, s.handle, tokenstore.EncodeTokenWithExpiration(t.AccessToken, expiresIn)); err != nil {
94			return fmt.Errorf("store access token: %w", err)
95		}
96		return nil
97	}

244	// RefreshedLoginToken returns context c's login JWT, transparently re-minting
245	// an expired one from the stored refresh token. It is the convenience form of
246	// NewRefreshingLoginProvider for callers that want a single token now (e.g.
247	// `auth status` / `logout`, which must report a refreshable session as alive
248	// rather than telling the user to re-login). The insecure-HTTP decision mirrors
249	// the control-plane resolver: loopback cores and the --insecure-http-auth
250	// opt-in are permitted, everything else requires https.
251	//
252	// Errors preserve the tokenmanager sentinels (ErrReauthRequired when the
253	// session is genuinely dead, ErrNotLoggedIn when no credential is usable) so
254	// callers can branch on errors.Is.
255	func RefreshedLoginToken(ctx context.Context, c *contexts.Context) (string, error) {
256		if c == nil {
257			return "", errors.New("nil context")
258		}
259		provider, err := NewRefreshingLoginProvider(c, nil, insecureHTTPEnabled() || isLoopbackHTTP(c.CoreURL))
260		if err != nil {
261			return "", err
262		}
263		return provider(ctx)
264	}
265	
266	// NewRefreshingResourceProvider returns a provider that mints a bearer valid
267	// for resourceOrigin, by exchanging context c's login JWT at c's own core (RFC
268	// 8693). It is NewRefreshingLoginProvider's sibling for resource servers: where
269	// that returns the bare login JWT (the control plane / cluster cases, where the
270	// host is the core), this performs the token exchange the data API requires.
271	//
272	// Both the silent login-JWT re-mint and the exchange run through the shared
273	// per-context tokenmanager (newContextTokenManager). resourceOrigin must
274	// already be origin-only (no path). No audience is passed: the token manager
275	// defaults the RFC 8693 audience to the resource origin, which is exactly what
276	// the data API requires (aud == its base URI), so the audience is derived from
277	// the host being dialed rather than read from discovery. Exchanged tokens are
278	// cached in-process by the tokenmanager for the life of this process.
279	//
280	// transport carries the caller's TLS configuration; allowInsecureHTTP permits
281	// an http:// core/resource for loopback/dev.
282	func NewRefreshingResourceProvider(c *contexts.Context, resourceOrigin string, transport http.RoundTripper, allowInsecureHTTP bool) (func(context.Context) (string, error), error) {
283		mgr, err := newContextTokenManager(c, transport, allowInsecureHTTP)
284		if err != nil {
285			return nil, err
286		}
287		req := tokenmanager.TokenRequest{Resource: resourceOrigin}
288		return func(ctx context.Context) (string, error) {
289			tok, err := mgr.Token(ctx, req)
290			if mapped := contextReauthError(c, err); mapped != nil {
291				return "", mapped
292			}
293			if err != nil {
294				return "", fmt.Errorf("exchange token for %s: %w", resourceOrigin, err)
295			}
296			return tok, nil
297		}, nil
298	}

1	package tokenstore
2	
3	import (
4		"fmt"
5		"strings"
6		"time"
7	)
8	
9	// TokenExpirationSeparator separates the token from its expiration timestamp.
10	// Format: "token|expires_at_unix"
11	const TokenExpirationSeparator = "|"
12	
13	// TokenExpirationBuffer is how long before expiration we should refresh.
14	const TokenExpirationBuffer = 5 * time.Minute
15	
16	// EncodeTokenWithExpiration encodes a token with its expiration time as a
17	// "token|expires_at_unix" suffix. Callers must pass a positive expiresIn —
18	// the encoded suffix is the contract that tells future readers when to
19	// refresh, and a zero/negative TTL would record an immediately-expired
20	// token.
21	func EncodeTokenWithExpiration(token string, expiresIn int64) string {
22		expiresAt := time.Now().Unix() + expiresIn
23		return fmt.Sprintf("%s%s%d", token, TokenExpirationSeparator, expiresAt)
24	}
25	
26	// DecodeTokenWithExpiration decodes a token that may have an expiration timestamp.
27	// Returns the token and expiration time. If no expiration is encoded, returns
28	// the token as-is and a zero time.
29	func DecodeTokenWithExpiration(encoded string) (token string, expiresAt time.Time) {
30		idx := strings.LastIndex(encoded, TokenExpirationSeparator)
31		if idx == -1 {
32			return encoded, time.Time{}
33		}
34	
35		token = encoded[:idx]
36		var expiresAtUnix int64
37		if _, err := fmt.Sscanf(encoded[idx+1:], "%d", &expiresAtUnix); err != nil {
38			return encoded, time.Time{}
39		}
40		return token, time.Unix(expiresAtUnix, 0)
41	}
42	
43	// IsTokenExpiredOrExpiring checks if a token is expired or will expire soon.
44	// A zero expiresAt is treated as "unknown, assume expired".
45	func IsTokenExpiredOrExpiring(expiresAt time.Time) bool {
46		if expiresAt.IsZero() {
47			return true
48		}
49		return time.Now().Add(TokenExpirationBuffer).After(expiresAt)
50	}

---
name: auth-fixture-jwt-expiry-gotcha
description: Seeding a fake expired login for the CLI requires a parseable JWT — auth-go judges expiry from the exp claim, not the store's encoded "|<unix>" suffix
metadata:
  type: reference
---

To make the CLI attempt a refresh (and so exercise the refresh/re-login error
paths) with a hand-seeded token store, the access token must be a JWT that
`tokens.ParseClaims` accepts, with `exp` in the past. auth-go's
`tokenmanager.coreTokenExpired` (v0.5.2, `tokenmanager.go`) returns **false** on
a parse failure or a missing `exp` — opaque tokens are treated as live and never
re-minted — so the `token|<unix>` expiry the CLI's own tokenstore encodes is
ignored for this decision.

Practical effect: a fixture JWT with a non-base64 signature segment (e.g.
`hdr.payload.sig`) silently parses as opaque, the CLI skips the refresh, and the
request goes out with the stale token — you end up debugging the wrong code
path. Encode all three segments base64url (see `makeJWT` in
`cmd/entire/cli/auth/contexts_test.go`).

Isolating a spawned `entire` for this kind of repro: `ENTIRE_CONFIG_DIR`
(holds `contexts.json`), `XDG_CACHE_HOME`, `ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE=file`,
`ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE_PATH`. The file store's format is
`{"<service>": {"<handle>": "<secret>"}}` with service
`entire-core:<core-url>` and the refresh token under
`entire-core:<core-url>:refresh`.

Yes, still a thing on `main` — this worktree is exactly at `origin/main` (43425357c, 0 commits behind), and I reproduced your message verbatim before changing anything:

```
resolve mirror placements: security "BearerAuth": security source "BearerAuth": refresh login token: refresh token: Post "https://localhost:8180/oauth/token": dial tcp [::1]:8180: connect: connection refused
```

Now, same command against the same dead core (real binary, isolated config pointing at `https://localhost:8180`):

```
resolve mirror placements: cannot reach the login server for "local" (https://localhost:8180): dial tcp [::1]:8180: connect: connection refused; run `entire login` to sign in again, or `entire auth use <context>` to switch to another login
```

**What was wrong, and what changed**

1. Nothing named the login context that chose that host, and nothing pointed at a fix. `cmd/entire/cli/auth/refresh.go` already reworded the two re-auth sentinels with the context name + core; transport failures fell through to a bare `refresh login token: %w`. Added `contextUnreachableError` alongside it, gated on `*url.Error` (a 4xx from the token endpoint is a credential problem and keeps its own text; cancel/deadline excluded). Both the login-JWT path and the STS exchange path now route through one `contextAuthError`.

2. `security "BearerAuth": security source "BearerAuth":` is ogen-generated (`oas_client_gen.go`, `oas_security_gen.go`) — it names the OpenAPI scheme that failed to resolve, which no user can act on. New `coreapi.StripSecurityWrapping` peels it *structurally*: it decomposes each link into the prefix its wrapper added plus the message it wrapped, and drops only a prefix that is itself a generated wrapper — so the same words inside an API problem detail survive. Applied in `renderCoreError` (the documented central mapper) and in main.go's print branch as the backstop for paths like `repo clone` that don't route through it.

3. While verifying I found the sibling case: same dead core, but the access token hasn't expired yet, so the request itself fails. That read `do request: Get "…": cross-juris transport: base round trip: dial tcp …`. `http.Client` already wraps every RoundTripper error in a `*url.Error` naming method and URL, so those two internal prefixes were pure padding — dropped (the other failure sites in that file keep theirs, they name real mechanisms). It now reads:

```
resolve mirror placements: do request: Get "https://localhost:8180/api/v1/mirrors/placements?owner=entirehq&provider=github&repo=wad-san-jose-booth-experience": dial tcp [::1]:8180: connect: connection refused
```

I left that path's remaining rough edges alone rather than expanding scope: `do request` is ogen's wording and does distinguish send-from-decode, and this path doesn't name the login context at all (the transport layer doesn't know it — plumbing the context name down there is a bigger change). Say the word if you want it to get the same treatment as the refresh path.

`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

## Verdict: nothing in this diff is worth changing for efficiency.

Every new code path is error-only or once-per-process, and the one claim worth checking hard (startup cost) turns out to be a non-event. Details, including the two things I expected to be findings and aren't:

### 1. `internal/coreapi/security_wrap.go:14` — package-level `regexp.MustCompile`: no startup regression. Verified, do not change.
The premise that the new `main.go` import pulls `coreapi` onto the hook path is **false**. `cmd/entire/cli` already imports `internal/coreapi` from ~28 non-test files (`corecmd.go:20`, `auth.go:18`, `repo.go:13`, `repo_mirror.go:20`, …), and `main.go` has always imported `cmd/entire/cli`. `go list -deps ./cmd/entire/cli | grep coreapi` hits — independent of the diff. So `coreapi`'s init already ran on every `entire` invocation, `entire hooks` included. The new import adds zero packages to the binary.

`regexp` is likewise already in `coreapi`'s own dep closure (`ogenregex` at `oas_cfg_gen.go:13`), so no new package init and no new binary bytes either.

Cost of the one added pattern compile: **2.8–4.8µs**, against a measured **58ms** per `entire version` (20 warm runs). That is ~0.008% of startup, and the repo already compiles ~70 package-level regexps at init. A hand-rolled matcher (`CutPrefix "security "` → `TrimPrefix "source "` → quoted-check) benches at 8.6ns/match vs 135ns with no init cost, but it buys single-digit microseconds once per process and costs readability. Don't.

### 2. `internal/coreapi/security_wrap.go:33-45` — the peel loop is genuinely O(n²), and it does not matter.
The quadratic behaviour is real, and for a non-obvious reason worth recording: for chains built by `fmt.Errorf`, `Error()` is a precomputed field read, so re-rendering is free. But the security segments come from **go-faster/errors** (`oas_security_gen.go:199,207`), whose `wrapError.Error()` is `fmt.Sprint(e)` → recursive `FormatError` over the entire tail through the `fmt` reflection machinery, allocating a fresh full string per call. So on exactly the chains this function targets, each link's message is re-rendered from scratch.

Measured on go-faster chains: reported real shape (depth 4, 2 go-faster links) **1.33µs**; synthetic depth 5 **2.5µs**; depth 20 **26.5µs** — 4× depth for 10.5× cost, confirming superlinear.

Path: error-only. Both call sites (`main.go:133`, `corecmd.go:650`) sit inside `err != nil` branches and run at most once per process, immediately before printing and exiting.

The cheaper alternative works — hoist `innerMsg := inner.Error()` and carry it forward as the next iteration's `curMsg`: **1.33µs → 0.83µs** on the real chain, 26.5µs → 13.9µs at depth 20. That is 500ns once per failed command against a 58ms process. **Not worth it**; the current form also reads more plainly as "decompose each link independently."

### 3. `cmd/entire/cli/auth/refresh.go:207-223` — 3 extra chain walks + a duplicated `TrimRight` on the error path; ~2ns on the success path. Negligible.
`contextAuthError` runs `contextReauthError` (2 `errors.Is` walks + `strings.TrimRight(c.CoreURL, "/")`) and then `contextUnreachableError` (1 `errors.As` + 2 more `errors.Is` walks + a second `TrimRight` of the same value) — 5 walks of the same ~4-link chain, and one `TrimRight` computed twice. Each walk is ~10-40ns; `TrimRight` with a one-byte cutset returns a substring with no allocation. ~100ns total, once, on the error path.

The path that actually runs per request is the success path, and there the addition is ~2ns: `result()` and the resource-provider closure call `contextAuthError(c, nil)` unconditionally, and `errors.As(nil, &urlErr)` returns at its first line — I checked go1.26.5 `errors/wrap.go`, the `err == nil` short-circuit precedes all reflection and the target-type panics. No reflection, no walk. Merging the two predicates to share one walk and one `TrimRight` would trade three separately-documented functions for ~100ns before the process exits. Leave it.

### 4. `cmd/entire/cli/corecmd.go:650` + `cmd/entire/main.go:133` — the strip runs twice per core-command error. ~1µs. Negligible.
`renderCoreError` returns a `*strippedError`, which `main.go` then hands back to `StripSecurityWrapping`. The second pass isn't free: it costs one `inner.Error()` — a full go-faster render of the original chain — before `CutSuffix` fails and it bails. ~1µs, once, per failed command. A two-line `if _, ok := err.(*strippedError); ok { return err }` guard at the top would erase it, but the backstop-in-`main` design is the right shape and the magnitude doesn't justify special-casing.

### 5. Closure/retention: nothing extended. No finding.
`NewRefreshingResourceProvider`'s returned closure already captured `c` (it called `contextReauthError(c, err)`); swapping in `contextAuthError(c, err)` changes neither the capture set nor its size. `RefreshingLoginCredential.result` reads `c.context`, a field the long-lived struct already holds. And `contextUnreachableError` wraps `urlErr.Err` rather than `urlErr`, so the returned error retains only the freshly formatted message plus the transport cause — the `*url.Error` and its `Op`/`URL` strings become collectible, which is marginally *better* for retention than wrapping the `*url.Error` would have been. The error itself is printed and then the process exits.

### 6. New tests: cheap, no sleeps, no network waits. No finding.
- `refresh_test.go:213` (`UnreachableCore`) measured **0.01s**. It obtains an unreachable address by binding `127.0.0.1:0` and closing it, so the dial returns an immediate loopback `ECONNREFUSED` instead of waiting on a timeout — the correct construction. No `time.Sleep`, no retry loop, no fixed wait.
- `refresh_test.go:270` (`RejectedRefreshIsNotUnreachable`) measured **0.00s**. Its `httptest.NewServer` is one loopback listener (sub-millisecond) and matches the pattern already used by `ForceRefreshesRejectedFreshToken` and `RefreshesAndRotates` in the same file. A canned `RoundTripper` would skip the listener and save microseconds while diverging from the file's convention — not worth it.
- `security_wrap_test.go` is pure in-memory, `t.Parallel()` on parent and every subtest, **0.00s**.
- The two auth tests correctly omit `t.Parallel()`: `tokenstore.UseFileBackendForTesting` is process-global, and no test in `refresh_test.go` is parallel. No reclaimable parallelism.

`internal/coreapi/cross_juris_transport.go:216` drops a `fmt.Errorf` wrap, removing one allocation and one format per transport failure. Error path, so immaterial — but it is work removed, not added.</result>

<result>## Findings (ordered by value)

**1. `internal/coreapi/security_wrap.go:59-69` — two `CutSuffix` steps + two `break`s collapse into one.**
The `prefix` intermediate exists only to be trimmed of `": "` on the next line. The two conditions are algebraically the same condition: "outer message ends with `inner.Error()`" AND "the remainder ends with `": "`" ⟺ "outer message ends with `": " + inner.Error()`", and the resulting `segment` is byte-identical.
Cost: 11 lines and two exit points where one suffices, plus a reader holding `prefix` (with trailing `": "`) and `segment` (without) apart in their head — the sort of pair that invites a future edit to use the wrong one.
Simpler form (keep the existing comment verbatim above it):
```go
segment, ok := strings.CutSuffix(cur.Error(), ": "+inner.Error())
if !ok {
    break
}
```
Verified: I copied `security_wrap.go` + `security_wrap_test.go` into a scratch module, applied exactly this change, and the diff's own tests pass unchanged. Loses nothing (one extra small string concat per link).

**2. `cmd/entire/cli/auth/refresh.go:215-218` — the `urlErr.Err != nil` fallback is unreachable and contradicts the comment directly above it.**
Every `*url.Error` a caller can observe here comes from `http.Client.Do`; both construction sites in `net/http/client.go` (:603, :633) always set a non-nil `Err`, all four `uerr(...)` calls pass a non-nil error, and `net/url`'s three sites do too.
Cost: 4 lines that make a reader hunt for the case where a `*url.Error` has no cause — and in that (impossible) case the branch wraps `urlErr` itself, producing exactly the "message repeats the core URL" outcome the doc comment at :204-206 says the design avoids. A defensive branch that defeats its own documented invariant is worse than none.
Simpler form: drop the rebind and pass `urlErr.Err` directly to `fmt.Errorf`. Honest loss: if some third-party transport ever hand-built `&url.Error{Err: nil}`, `%w` renders `%!w(<nil>)` instead of the `url.Error`'s own text. If you want a guard anyway, the one-line `if urlErr.Err == nil { return nil }` (fall through to the caller's own wording) is cheaper and preserves the invariant.

**3. `cmd/entire/cli/auth/refresh.go:153-163` — `contextAuthError` is a pure-delegation wrapper worth folding away.**
Its whole body is "call A; else call B". Grep confirms `contextReauthError` and `contextUnreachableError` now have no caller other than this wrapper and no direct tests, so the split buys no testability.
Cost: a third function in a chain of three, and a 5-line doc comment whose second half ("Returns nil for everything else, leaving the caller to wrap the residual error in its own terms (refresh vs exchange)") is copied near-verbatim from `contextReauthError`'s comment at :169-171 — two places now describe the same contract, and a future third mapper means updating both.
Simpler form: rename `contextReauthError` → `contextAuthError` and end its `switch` with `return contextUnreachableError(c, err)`. Both call sites (:256, :339) stay exactly as the diff has them, `contextUnreachableError` keeps its own (valuable) doc block, and `coreURL := strings.TrimRight(c.CoreURL, "/")` gets computed once for both branches instead of once per function. Net −1 function, −6 lines, no behavior change.
Conservative caveat: if a third mapper is imminent, the composition point earns its keep — at two it does not.

Cost: `net.ListenConfig` + two error branches to obtain a dead address, when the sibling test two functions down already imports `httptest`.
Simpler form:
```go
// A port nobody is listening on: start a server, take its URL, stop it.
srv := httptest.NewServer(http.HandlerFunc(func(http.ResponseWriter, *http.Request) {}))
coreURL := srv.URL
srv.Close()
```
Drops the `net` import. Verified in a scratch module (5 runs): a GET against a closed `httptest` server's URL unwraps to `syscall.ECONNREFUSED`, same as the released-listener trick, and rests on the same "just-released port stays free" assumption.

**5. `cmd/entire/cli/auth/refresh_test.go:228-245` vs `281-298` — 18 lines of identical seeding between the two new tests.**
The blocks differ only in the core URL, the transport argument, and the context name. Note this matches pre-existing local style (:106-120, :130-159, :184-198 all copy it), so this is optional — but the two *new* functions are the closest pair in the file and are the cheapest place to break the pattern before a fourth copy lands (`mise run dup`'s advisory threshold-50 pass will likely see it).
Simpler form: one helper in this file —
```go
// seedExpiredLogin seeds an expired access token plus an "entr_old" refresh
// token for coreURL and returns a login provider for a context named name.
func seedExpiredLogin(t *testing.T, name, coreURL string, transport http.RoundTripper) func(context.Context) (string, error)
```
— after which each new test is fixture + one call + its own assertions, and `TestNewRefreshingLoginProvider_ExpiredNoRefresh` can adopt it later.
Do **not** table-drive these two: they need different fixtures (dead port vs live 400-ing server) and opposite assertions, so a table would need a per-case setup closure — more machinery than it removes.

Simpler form: one `strings.Contains(got, fmt.Sprintf("cannot reach the login server for %q (%s)", "local", coreURL))` (pins the three together, in order), plus the two existing hint checks (`entire login`, `entire auth use <context>`) as plain `Contains` calls — 5 checks become 3, and the first is stricter.

There is no dot anywhere in `security_wrap.go`; the row asserts that an empty scheme name still matches `[^"]*` and leaves no stray separator. Reads like a leftover from an earlier join implementation.
Cost: a reader greps for "dot", finds nothing, and can't tell what the row is defending — and the row's real subject is an input ogen cannot emit (schemes always come from the spec).
Simpler form: rename to `"empty scheme name still matches"`, or drop the row.

**8. `internal/coreapi/security_wrap_test.go:51` — `"wrapper is stripped when it is the only segment"` describes an axis the row above it also has.**
The row at :46 (`security "SessionAuth"`) is *also* the only segment; the actual distinction is the optional `source ` group in the regexp.
Cost: three near-identical rows (:46, :51, :73) all expecting `"boom"` with names that don't separate them — someone tidying up will delete the wrong one and silently drop regexp coverage.
Simpler form: rename to something like `"the security source form is stripped too"`. Keep all three rows; this is naming only.

**9. `internal/coreapi/security_wrap_test.go:19, 25` — `StripSecurityWrapping(err)` is called twice.** Assign once (`stripped := StripSecurityWrapping(err)`) and use it for both the message and the `errors.Is` check. Micro-nit.

- **`strippedError` cannot be `fmt.Errorf`.** No `fmt.Errorf` verb produces an error whose message is *independent* of the wrapped error's text while still unwrapping to it; a 6-line type is the only shape. (It is now the third instance of the `msg`+`err` pair — `auth.reauthError`, `coreapi.strippedError`, plus the test's `rewrittenError`. content.text:
Cleanup applied and verified. Four reviewers, deduped to 11 fixes and 5 skips.

**Fixed**

*Altitude — the fix didn't reach every render site.* My claim that main.go was "the single place errors get printed" was wrong: the search TUI captures `msg.err.Error()` into its Bubble Tea model (`search_tui.go:335,354,396`) and the command then returns nil, so `entire search` — the most interactive command — still showed the raw `security "BearerAuth"` chain. Both strip call sites are now one named choke point, `cli.RenderUserFacingError` (`errors.go`), called from main.go, `renderCoreError`, and the three TUI sites. main.go no longer imports `internal/coreapi`.

Also corrected the two comments that described *each other* as the backstop. The real asymmetry: main.go's default branch is the choke point; `renderCoreError`'s copy is load-bearing for exactly one shape — the mirror-create wizard prints its own error and returns a `SilentError`, so main.go never renders it.

*Altitude — scope of the unreachable-core message.* Narrowed the doc claim from "any command that needs a token" to the paths that *mint* one, and named the deeper fix (carry the context name on `auth.ControlPlaneTarget` so the coreapi client can reword its own transport failures next to `CoreOrigin()`). That's the live-token gap I flagged earlier; it's now written down where the next reader will hit it.

*Simplification.* Folded `contextAuthError`'s pure-delegation layer into the renamed `contextReauthError` → one function, `coreURL` trimmed once, −6 lines. Dropped the `urlErr.Err != nil` rebind — unreachable (`http.Client` always sets it) and, in the impossible case, it produced exactly the URL-repetition the doc says it avoids. Collapsed the peeler's two `CutSuffix` steps into one (`CutSuffix(cur.Error(), ": "+inner.Error())`).

*Reuse / tests.* Replaced the 9-line `net.ListenConfig` port dance with the repo's `httptest.NewServer` + `Close()` idiom (drops the `net` import); extracted `seedExpiredLogin`, collapsing ~18 duplicated seeding lines from both new tests; tightened the 5-element `Contains` loop into 3 checks with phrase + context name + host pinned together and in order (stricter, not just shorter); fixed two misleading table-case names and a doubled `StripSecurityWrapping` call.

**Skipped**

- **Extracting a shared transport-error predicate** with `isRecapNetworkError` (`recap_errors.go:69`). Real duplication, but `auth` can't import `cli` and `coreapi` imports `auth`, so reuse needs a new leaf package for 6 lines. Left a comment cross-referencing it and recording why no separate DNS tier is needed here (`http.Client` wraps `*net.DNSError` in a `*url.Error` too).
- **Generation-level fix for the ogen noise.** The reviewer verified there is none: the wrapper text is hard-wired in ogen's embedded templates via an unexported loader, with no `--templates` flag, config option, or feature toggle. Render-time is the right depth.
- **All efficiency findings.** The peel loop is genuinely O(n²) (go-faster's `Error()` re-renders per call) — 1.3µs on the real chain, error path only. The new `regexp.MustCompile` adds no startup cost: `coreapi` was already imported by ~28 files in `cli`, so its init always ran.
- **The `//nolint:wrapcheck`** — the error comes from `net/http`, which the `ignore-package-globs` entry doesn't cover, and per-site directives are the established convention (5 precedents).
- **Adopting `seedExpiredLogin` in the two pre-existing tests** that share the same block, and table-driving the two new tests (different fixtures, opposite assertions).

`mise run fmt && mise run lint` clean; `mise run test:ci` exit 0 with the canary green (56 + 4); the reported command re-verified end to end against a dead core after the refactor. One note: the efficiency reviewer ran a `git stash` mid-review — I checked, the tree is intact and no stash entry was added.
